title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Power
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: A third Citrix NetScaler zero-day is under attack as exploitation of the first two widens; patching does not evict an intruder
items.content_text: Citrix confirmed on 27 September that two NetScaler ADC and Gateway flaws were exploited before patches existed: CVE-2026-88771, which lets an unauthenticated attacker run commands on default configurations, and CVE-2026-88772, a memory flaw reachable when DTLS is enabled, the default on VPN virtual servers (both CVSS v4 9.5). Mandiant counts “dozens” of victims in government, technology, finance, telecom, education and professional services; Arctic Wolf counts at least 78, and researcher Kevin Beaumont more than 100 by his own tracking. Mandiant calls the actors suspected state-sponsored and names no group. Intruders planted web shells, created a rogue superuser account and stole appliance configurations, and Mandiant warns that upgrading alone does not remove that access. On 4 October CISA added a third flaw, CVE-2026-88779 (CVSS v4 8.7), after Citrix reported targeted attacks causing denial of service on SAML-configured appliances. watchTowr reproduced it as a crash-only bug and suspects it is used to knock appliances over to speed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771; one researcher reported signs of code execution on a honeypot, which Citrix has not confirmed. No power-sector victim has been named, but NetScaler often fronts contractor and field-staff access at utilities, so an unhunted appliance is a possible first hop toward EMS, SCADA and substation networks.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Citrix bulletins CTX697096 and CTX697174; CISA KEV listings 27 Sep and 4 Oct 2026 (primary); Mandiant, Arctic Wolf and watchTowr findings reported by SecurityWeek, Cybersecurity Dive and Help Net Security
_otthreatfeed.date_note: First two flaws confirmed 27 Sep 2026; third flaw KEV-listed 4 Oct 2026; watchTowr denial-of-service finding 5 Oct 2026

items.title: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager authentication bypass CVE-2026-76504 was exploited as a zero-day; there is no workaround
items.content_text: Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-76504 (CVSS 9.8) on 30 September: Catalyst SD-WAN Manager mishandles URI encoding, so a crafted HTTP request can bypass an API authentication rule and give a remote, unauthenticated attacker administrative access. Cisco says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in September, and CISA added the flaw to KEV the same day with a 3 October federal deadline, now passed. Cisco revised the advisory on 2 October. There is no workaround; a temporary Live Protect shield gives partial protection but may block some legitimate users. BleepingComputer counts this as the fifth exploited SD-WAN zero-day of 2026. No actor, victim or sector has been named. SD-WAN Manager pushes policy to the overlay that many utilities use to link offices, plants and substations, so administrative access to it is a position from which traffic paths toward field sites could be changed (editorial assessment).

items.title: Three clusters are exploiting Cisco firewall-manager flaws CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-20316; one shares tooling with Sandworm
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079, a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass that lets an unauthenticated attacker run scripts and potentially gain root on Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center, is being exploited; CISA added it to KEV with a 12 September deadline, now passed. Cisco Talos describes three clusters. UAT-12197 deployed a web shell and stole credentials. UAT-11823 used both CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-20316 (CVSS 5.3, low-privilege remote login) to drop reverse shells and then Cyclops Blink malware, with tooling that Talos says overlaps with the Sandworm APT actor — an overlap, not a government attribution. UAT-11988, a ransomware operator, used CVE-2026-20316 and living-off-the-land tools for reconnaissance before deploying Qilin ransomware. Cisco released hotfixes for both flaws, and Talos said a broader hardening release would follow in the week of 14 September; Talos last updated its post on 21 September and names no victims or sectors. FMC configures the firewalls that separate corporate networks from generation, substation and DER control.

items.title: Fortinet FortiMail flaw CVE-2026-104286 was exploited before a fix existed; Fortinet’s 5 October update now lists fixed releases
items.content_text: Fortinet published advisory FG-IR-26-175 on 1 October for CVE-2026-104286 (CVSS 9.8), a path-traversal flaw in FortiMail that lets an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files on the appliance with crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests. Fortinet says the flaw has been reported exploited in the wild, and CISA added it to KEV on 1 October with a 4 October deadline. No fixed build was available at disclosure; Fortinet’s 5 October update lists 8.0.2, 7.6.7 and 7.4.9, and tells 7.2 users to move to the 7.4 branch or later. Fortinet still urges its workarounds: turn off the IBE feature, restrict the webmail interface to trusted networks, and block POST requests to /ibe paths that contain “../”. No actor or victims have been disclosed. FortiMail sits on the corporate side rather than in control networks, but a compromised mail gateway is a trusted platform for phishing operations and engineering staff (editorial assessment).

items.title: CenterPoint Energy confirms customer data was taken; a hacker claims about 7.5 million records and threatens “infrastructure” next
items.content_text: CenterPoint Energy told the SEC on 15 September that an unauthorized third party obtained personal information relating to a portion of its customers through one of its externally facing systems. Three days earlier a threat actor had posted a 2.5 GB archive on a cybercrime forum, claiming about 7.5 million records and adding: “next time we won’t simply pull data, we’ll start attacking the main infrastructure.” CenterPoint says the incident has not affected the delivery of electric or gas service; it has not confirmed the record count, and no vulnerability, intrusion vector or actor identity has been disclosed. SecurityWeek cautions that hackers often exaggerate and that the data’s validity is unconfirmed, and notes this is not the first CenterPoint data incident. This reads as an IT-side data breach, not an OT compromise — but the actor’s stated intent is a reason for other utilities to check that customer-facing systems are properly segmented from anything that touches control-system networks.
tags: Incident — Confirmed customer-data breach at a US electric & gas utility

items.title: CISA and FBI: a compromised ICS integrator held utilities’ SCADA data — limit what yours can reach
items.content_text: CISA and the FBI released a joint fact sheet on 24 September, “Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators.” Its motivating case: in March–April 2025, foreign actors inside a US industrial automation company that does system integration and SCADA programming for customers including power utilities and transportation entities searched for “customers” and “SCADA” and staged nine archives of about 800 files — customer SCADA information, ICS device details and schematics — for exfiltration. The agencies do not name the company, the actor or its country, and do not say any utility was breached. Their advice: write security and supply-chain requirements into integrator contracts, apply least privilege, route remote access through monitored, on-demand channels, know what data integrators hold and where, and be able to operate if an integrator is compromised.
tags: Threat Intelligence — Joint CISA/FBI guidance drawn from a compromised ICS integrator

items.title: A predictable session ID lets an attacker bypass authentication on Siemens’ Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relay
items.content_text: Siemens published advisory SSA-142885 on 8 September as part of that month’s ICS Patch Tuesday batch. It covers 15 vulnerabilities in the Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relay, with a top CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8: authentication bypass through predictable session identifiers, plus denial of service, privilege escalation and, for someone with physical access, memory corruption and unsigned code execution in maintenance mode. All versions before V2.70 are affected. No in-the-wild exploitation or public exploit code has been reported. Protection relays like this trip breakers to protect equipment during faults; an attacker with unauthenticated access could, in principle, alter settings or block a legitimate trip, though doing so would first require network reach to the relay.
tags: Advisory — Protection relay authentication bypass, no known exploitation

items.title: Schneider Electric PowerLogic T300 substation RTU has a root privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-77120 (CVSS 8.7)
items.content_text: Schneider Electric’s September ICS Patch Tuesday release on 8 September included a high-severity OS command-injection flaw (CWE-78), CVE-2026-77120, in the PowerLogic T300 — the platform formerly sold as the Easergy T300 RTU — in versions 2.9.8-5620 and earlier. Exploitation needs authenticated SSH access with high privileges, after which an attacker could escalate to root and run administrative functions; the advisory is SEVD-2026-251-02. The same release covered a CVSS 9.2 authentication flaw in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers (CVE-2026-3869), which matters to plant automation at generation sites. Neither is reported as exploited or in KEV. The T300 flaw is a post-access risk rather than a remote entry point, so the priority is controlling who holds SSH credentials on substation RTUs.

items.title: ABB’s PCM600 relay-engineering tool has two local flaws and no fixed version yet, only configuration workarounds
items.content_text: CISA published advisory ICSA-26-274-03 on 1 October for ABB’s Protection and Control IED Manager PCM600, versions 2.14 and earlier; ABB’s own advisories are dated 28 September. CVE-2026-15952 (CVSS v3.1 6.4, v4 7.1) is an incorrect permission assignment: PCM600’s Scheduler Service runs as LocalSystem while granting permissions to standard users, so an attacker with local access and valid credentials could escalate privileges. CVE-2026-15953 (v3.1 5.0, v4 5.6) is a path traversal in archive processing that could write files outside the intended directory; it needs local access and user interaction. CISA lists the Energy sector and reports no known public exploitation. ABB has released no fixed version, only mitigations. Neither flaw is remotely exploitable, but PCM600 is the tool engineers use to manage protection and control IEDs, so the workstations it runs on deserve the same care as the relays (editorial assessment).

items.title: DOE’s request for information on foreign-equipment risk in the bulk-power system closes this Friday, 9 October
items.content_text: Executive Order 14421, signed 26 August, declares a national emergency over the security of the US bulk-power system and authorizes the Department of Energy to prohibit, condition or unwind transactions involving foreign-produced bulk-power equipment tied to covered foreign entities. Coverage includes transmission at 69 kV and above, generation needed for reliability, and substation, control-room and generating-station equipment such as transformers, inverters, battery storage and industrial control systems; DOE may also set conditions on previously installed equipment and must issue implementing rules within 120 days. On 9 September DOE published a Federal Register request for information asking utilities, manufacturers, software developers and integrators about equipment definitions, foreign-entity identification, risk criteria, existing-equipment mitigation, remote access and domestic supply. Responses are voluntary and due 9 October 2026; DOE says the request is for information and planning and is not itself a proposed rule.

items.title: DOE launches a $100 million cybersecurity technical-assistance partnership for cooperative, municipal and small electric utilities
items.content_text: DOE’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response (CESER) announced on 1 October the $100 million Rural and Municipal Utility Cybersecurity (RMUC) Advanced Cybersecurity Technical Assistance partnership, administered by DOE’s partnership intermediary ConnectWerx. Applicant organizations must have formal partnerships with at least six qualifying electric utilities: cooperatives, municipal utilities or small investor-owned utilities. Funded work covers assessments and planning, workforce training and certification, exercises, tool implementation, verification and validation, and threat-information sharing. DOE’s announcement gives no application deadline and points applicants to ConnectWerx for details. It creates no new requirement, but for utilities without in-house OT security staff it is a route to outside assessment and exercise help.
